FINANCIAL NEEDS, 

For the adequate support of the growing work of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association of the City of Montreal and its 
Branches, an enlarged regular contributing constituency is 
needed. Contributions for current expenses towards the 
support of any Department will be gratefully acknowledged. 
We would present the following pressing needs :— 

For Railroad Branch at Point St. Charles. 

For French Branch. 

For addition to Building on Dominion Square, so as to 
enlarge Physical and Educational privileges. (The 
Association owns the necessary land), 

For athletic grounds fo? out-door games. 

For an enlarged Library from 5,000 to 10,000 volumes. 

For an endowment for the Educational work in evening 
classes and lectures.

AN HISTORICAL RESUME 


OF THE 


YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. 


The Young Men’s Christian Association had its origin in the 
desire of a few earnest young men, employés in a London drapery 
house, to lead their associates to Christ and aid them in living pure 
and useful lives. This occurred in 1844, and the first great aim of 
the organization has not changed, but simply broadened in ways and 
means from that day to this. The active efforts of the London 
association in connection with the great Industrial Exposition of 
1851 gained the attention of foreign visitors, and spread a knowledge 
of the movement to other lands. In North America the first organi- 
zatious were effected at Montreal and Boston, the former the 2Ist 
November, and the latter the 29th of December, 1851. The first 
delegated convention met in Buffalo, June 7, 1854, ten years and a 
day after the organization of the London society. It resulted in 
the formation of a voluntary confederation, with provisions for a 
central committee and an annual convention. During the next six 
years there was a gradual growth in numbers, and while there was 
much that was crude and ill-defined and little uniformity in methods, 
active and earnest work was done and the foundation laid for a more 
perfect superstructure. The civil war of 1861-65 wiped out a greav 
majority of the American associations ; the U.S. Christian Com- 
mission, however, organized through their agency, accomplished a 
beneficent work, sending out during the war 5,000 Christian workers 
to the camps and hospitals, and distributing over $5,000,000 in 
money and stores. The war also broke up the old confederation ; 
but a new general organization on a broader and stronger plan was 
formed at a convention held in Chicago in 1863, and the re-organ- 
ized work made rapid and substantial advancement. The evangelical 
test of active membership, a definite and all-round work for young 
men, the erection of well-adapted association homes, the employ- 
ment of trained officers, systematized effort for special classes of 
men, a more thorough general supervision through international 
and state or provincial organizations, each contributed to the unifi- 
cation, growth and efficiency of the following years. 

The International Committee, numbering at first but five, has 
increased to forty-three members, representing all sections of the 
United States and Canada. Its secretarial staff, field, departmental 
and office, has grown from one to forty, besides eighteen in the 
foreign mission field. The individual associations have always pos- 
sessed absolute autonomy, except that a constitutional provision 
restricting voting and holding office to members of evangelical 
churches is necessary to representation in the International Conven- 
tion, to which all affiliating associations ‘may send delegates. These 
conventions were held annually till 1877, since which they have been 
biennial. Through this body the associations appoint, instruct and 
control the International committee, the important central agency 


4 


of general supervision. The state and provincial organizations 
supplement the international agency in the work of general super- 
vision. Called into existence in 1866, there are now thirty-five com- 
mittees, embracing forty-nine states and provinces, and employing a 
field and office force of fifty secretaries. About thirty state and 
provincial conventions are held each year. The local associations, 
city and town, student, railroad, etc., number 1,439, with an agere- 
gate membership of over 255,000. The number of men on working 
cominittees is 35,070. In 1871 there were only twelve or fifteen paid 
officers; in 1900 there are 1,309. Two well-equipped training 
schools graduate annually from twenty to twenty-five men as general 
secretaries and physical directors, 

The first association building was erected in 1867 ; ten years later 
there were twenty-two ; during 1899 nearly forty buildings were 
erected. There are now 359 buildings, valued at $21,620,230. Very 
many of these are fine structures, comparing favorably with other 
public buildings in their respective cities, and thoroughly adapted as 
to location, arrangement and equipment for their varied work and 
the special classes to be reached, The four leading features in the 
local work are the religious, the educational, the social, and the 
physical. Last year 56,000 religious meetings for men were 
reported, with a total attendance of 2,500,000. In 1866, thirteen out 
of fifty-nine associations reported Bible classes; in 1900 818 asso- 
ciations reported 40,830 Bible and training class sessions, with a total 
attendance of 496,141. The recent organization of a Bible study 
department of the International Committee, and the adoption of 
uniform and graded courses of study is greatly stimulating Bible 
study in the city associations. Similarly the appointment eight years 
ago of an International Educational Secretary, and a thorough 
reorganization of this department, including the adoption of uniform 
graded courses of study for evening classes, and a system of inter- 
national examinations, has greatly promoted and improved the 
methods of the educational work. Classes are conducted by 350 
associations in fifty subjects, and 1,200 teachers give instruction to 
25,000 different young men. Reading rooms are reported by 763 
associations ; 632 libraries are reported, containing nearly 500,000 
volumes ; 172 literary societies have an average attendance of 5,071 ; 
596 associations report 3,993 lectures. In 1883, gymnasiums were 
reported by fifty associations ; there are now 500. The percentage 
of improvement in methods is still greater, the work being con- 
ducted largely on a scientific basis and under the guidance of 
technically educated and Christian physical directors, the aim 
being physical health, needed physical recreation and a symmetrical 
building up and training of the body for one’s life work. The 
associations are a leading force in the athletics of the continent, and 
their watch-cry of “clean sport” is favorably affecting other 
organizations, 

Work for students practically began in 1877; there are now 550 
student associations, with a membership of 32,000. The work is 
definite, well organized and an acknowledged and powerful factor 
in student life. Ten thousand five hundred are in the association 
Bible classes; 1,200 attend the four summer conferences. During 
the past twenty-two years 35,000 to 40,000 students have been led 
into the Christian life, and more than 5,000 into the Christian minis- 
try through this agency. Among the direct outgrowths of the work 
are the Student volunteer movement, through which more than 1,500 


0 


have already entered the foreign mission field, and the World’s 
Student Christian federation, through which the Christian students 
ombined in eleven national and international student 
organizations, and thus brought into helpful relationship and made 
a potent force for united moral and religious action. 

The work for railroad men began in 1872; five years later there 
were twenty associations. The work then grew more rapidly, 
although the past two oF three years have seen the most marked 
advance. There are now I51 associations, with a membership ot 
over 37,000. An association is usually placed at a focal point where 
its influence covers a large area. Sixty buildings are either owned 
by the associations or set apart for their use. During one month 
oi the past year eight associations were opened with new and fully 
equipped buildings valued at $75,000, and free of debt. In addition 
to the usual facilities, such special features as baths at all hours, 
lunch counter, rest rooms and temporary hospital adapt the work to 
the peculiar needs of railroad men. The corporations show a prac- 
tical sympathy by contributing over $175,000 annually to support the 
work, besides large amounts given towards new buildings. 

The Spanish-American war, and later the war in South Africa, 
opened to the associations a field of usefulness similar to that in 
1861 ; but the associations were now in such condition as to num- 
bers and organization that they were able to take up the work with 
great promptness and vigor. Within two months after President 
McKinley’s call for volunteers, forty association tents were in the 
field, in charge of sixty trained secretaries. Such was the work 
accomplished during the campaign that not only the soldiers but 
government officers demanded its continuance, and it has been made 
a permanent department. Men and equipments are now with the 
American troops in Cuba, Porto Rico and the Philippines, and with 
the Canadian Contingents in South Africa. The work is also being 
established at army posts in the United States, and among the 
enlisted men in the navy. A naval branch is in successful operation 
near the New York navy yard, and a building for its use will soon 
be erected at a cost of $250,000. A general naval association has 
been formed with membership tickets good at all naval branches 
and at associations in sea-port towns. Auxiliary branches are also 
being organized on the war ships and a naval temperance league has 
just been put in successful operation. 

In 1889, in response to urgent calls from the missionaries, the 
North American committee sent two secretaries to the foreign field 
to establish associations at strategic points and train native Christian 
young men for the secretaryship. The movement has succeeded and 
spread till the committee now has men at work in India, Ceylon, 
China, Japan and South America. Associations have been formed, 
buildings erected, national organizations effected and a strong and 
many-sided work built up. In the British countries the English 
secretaries and our own have worked together and money from 
friends in both England and North America has been contributed 
towards the enterprise.

ANNUAL MEETING. 


The Forty-ninth Annual Meeting of the Association was held on 
Thursday evening, May 17th, at 8 o'clock. The President, Mr. Chas. 
T. Williams, occupied the chair. The attendance of members and 
subscribers was unusually large. 

After devotional exercises, led by Mr. John Murphy, the Secretary 
was called upon to read the Annual Report of the Board of Directors. 
Mr. L. H. Packard, Treasurer, presented the Financial Statement on 
Current Expense and Property Account The Current Expense 


‘ Account showed a deficit of $324. Mr. James Wilson proposed that 


the members present wipe out this amount. $278 was subscribed by 
a “card collection,’ and the Treasurer reported that a friend would 
be responsible for the balance. 

On behalf of the young men, Mr. Wilson asked permission to 
present the honored and faithful Treasurer with an enlarged picture 
of the Dominion Square Building. In accepting the picture, Mr. 
Packard expressed his deep appreciation of the gift of the young 
men, and the great privilege he had enjoyed during his long years of 
connection with the Association. 

Mr. Alex. Arthur reported on behalf of the Young Men’s Debt 
Fund, that $1,000 had been received during the year, and that a 
iurther sum of $1,600 was guaranteed and payable before December 
Ist, 1900. 

The annual reports of the various Committees were presented by 
the Chairman of each Department, the reports being printed and 
circulated amongst the members present. 

On motion of Mr. R. C. Holden, the reports as presented were 
received and adopted, and ordered to be printed and issued to the 
members and subscribers. _ 

The election of seven Directors was proceeded with, and resulted 
as follows :— 

H. J. Mupecer, Joun W. Ross, So: Ps-Leer 
Dr. W. F. Hamitton, L. H. Packarp, C. W Brown, 
Cuartes Morton, 

Votes of thanks were presented to the “ Press” and the “ Ladies’ 
Committee,” for their helpful co-operation, 

The meeting then adjourned. 


Forty-Ninth Annual Report. 


In coming before the members of the Association at their 
Forty-ninth Annual Meeting, the Board of Directors are 
thankful to be able to report gratifying progress on several 
lines of work :— 

MorrcaceE Dest.—tst. The mortgage indebtedness on 
the Dominion Square Building was $51,130. This was not 
ad a very heavy annual burden, but it has stood inthe way 

the development of the Association, as the Directors feared 
to Pekend by means of branches, which the best interests of 
the work in the city required, while this heavy financial 
obligation rested upon them. They are happy to report that 
subscriptions have now been secured covering this entire 
amount, and they desire to express their deep sense of grati- 
tude to all the subscribers who have so cheerfully and gener- 
ously come to the assistance of the Association in this 
important matter. 

IMPROVEMENT Account, ETC.—2nd, An additional amount 
of $8,556.50, for necessary improvements, was also con- 
tracted two years ago, in converting the three upper floors of 
the Building into dormitories for young men, and for neces- 
sary changes required in the Gymnasium and Baths. The 
Directors are pleased to be able to report that subscriptions 
covering this amount have also been secured, and it is 
expected that before December, 1900, these amounts will be 
paid. So soon as this is accomplished, there will be issued a 
complete statement of subscriptions, both on the Building 
Iund and the Improvement Account, with other details. 

For the consideration of these most important matters the 
Directors and Finance Committee have held a weekly meet- 
ing for conference and prayer during the whole winter, and 


12 


they desire to acknowledge God’s goodness to them in this 
matter and the special blessing which He has granted to their 
efforts. 

RAILROAD BraNncH.—3rd. The report of the Railroad 
Branch at Point St. Charles, shows encouraging progress, in 
an enlarged membership, an enlarged use of the rest rooms 
and privileges, and the possibility during this current year of 
securing a Branch Building specially constructed to suit the 
needs of this work for Railroad men, and also for the young 
men in that section of the city who are not railroad employes. 
Through the promised generous co-operation of Mr. Chas. 
M. Hays, General Manager of the Grand Trunk Railway 
System, this will be possible. Plans are now being consid- 
ered for.this purpose. 

INCOME FROM MemBers.—4th. The income from members’ 
fees up to April 30th is $6,670.90. This shows an increase | 
of $223.65 over last year. This increase is largely due to 
the number of members taking sustaining tickets. Last year 
we reported 126 Sustaining members, to-day, 184, an increase 
of 58. The Directors are pleased to note that this increase 
from “Full” to “Sustaining” indicates a deeper apprecia- 
tion on the part of these members of the value of the Asso- 
ciation. For this result the thanks of the Board is tendered 
to the Membership Committee for faithful service rendered. 

5th. Notwithstanding the fact that $27,696 was received 
during the year on account of Building Fund, the Finance 
Committee secured $6,458.72 towards the current expenses 
of the Association, which is an increase of $277.22 over the 
amount received for regular subscriptions last year. The 
Directors would here tender the thanks of the Association to 
the many friends of this work in the city who have so cheer- 
fully contributed the necessary funds. 

For the informataion of members and subscribers it should 
be stated that the membership fees are not sufficient to meet 
the current expenses of the Association. If they were in- 
creased so as to cover the expense, the result would be that 
young men who most need the advantages offered would be 


als: 


excluded, and the large work which is now done for strangers 
and non-members would be necessarily restricted. 
VoLUNTEER WORKING Force.—6th, An important advance 
has been made in effective Committee work. This is not an 
Association of the Directors or the Executive Officials, but 
of the rank and file of the membership. It is the members’ 
Association, and the work is planned and carried out by 
twenty-four Committees, composed of about 130 members. 
There are also a number of members who render most valu- 
able service, who are not on Committees. With the exception 
of three or four of these Committees, there is a decided gain 
to report in the Committee service of the past year. More 
men have been trained, and the responsibility for the detaiis 
of the work has been more evenly distributed. It must never 
be forgotten that the present and future welfare of the Asso- 
ciation is bound up in its volunteer working force, and the 
membership should be carefully studied with the view of 
constantly increasing the number of such workers. The 
responsibility for the administration of the departments 
should be so fully carried by these volunteer workers, that 
even any change in the officers of the Association would not 
seriously interrupt or affect the progress of the work. 
Reticious WorK.—7th. The public religious work has 
been strengthened by the addition of two week night Bible 
Classes and a Men’s Meeting on Sunday afternoon. The 
personal religious work has also been carefully considered. 
Most cheering results are apparent in the lives of men who 
have been redeemed from the power of evil, but the preventive 
work is far the greatest, both in its extent and the results 
secured. The hundreds of young men who are shielded from 
evil during the formative period of their lives, from 16 to 20 
years of age, and directed towards useful and helpful service, 
may not be so apparent to the casual observer, but to the 
thoughtful man, this latter work is much less expensive and 
more far-reaching in its results on any community. 
REPRESENTATIVES WITH CANADIAN CONTINGENTS.—8th. 
Perhaps the most important advance which the past year has 


14 


to record, and one which will have the widest results, is 
part taken by this Association in the sending of representa. 
tives with the Canadian Contingents to South Africa. he 
Provincial Committee in Toronto, was communicated with 
and they immediately took the matter up, and through tha 
organization the Canadian Associations were interested, gs¢ 
that three men—Dr. H. G. Barrie, College Secretary, 
Toronto, Thos. F. Best, Secretary, Brantford, and Archie 
MacKellar, Assistant Secretary, Ottawa—are now in Sout} 
Africa representing the Associations with the Canadian Regi 
ments. This affords a most practical illustration as to hoy 
the work of the Association can be quickly adapted to larg 
bodies of men, even under the most difficult conditions. The 
results already secured abundantly justified the action of the 
Associations. 
We are glad to acknowledge the valuable services rendere 
by Lord Strathcona. The Department at Ottawa could onh 
grant our representatives permission to go as far as Capi 
Town, but when written to by our Secretary, Lord Strathcon: 
took the matter up with the British War Office, and secures 
the retention of our representatives with the Canadian Re 
ments when taken over by the British Army, and during thei 
service in Africa. About $800 was freely contributed by out 
members for this special work. ‘

Work FOR YOUNG Men iN Forercn Lanps.—oth. An 
advance has also been made in the work for foreign young 
men during the year. One of our members has undertaken 
the support of Galen M. Fisher, the International Secretary 
for the College Student work of Japan, and through another 
member the support of Robt. P. Wilder, as Travelling Col- 
lege Secretary for India, has been assured, and both of these 
men are now on the field. Through the collective and indi- 
vidual subscriptions of members this Association is now 
represented on the foreign field by :-— 

Davip McConaucuy, National Secretary of India. 
j. Camppect WuiITE, College Secretary, Calcutta. 
Rost. P. WriLpeER, College Secretary for India. 
GALEN M. Fisuer, College Secretary for Japan. 

In this important department we occupy a unique position 
in the Association brotherhood. 

CHANGES IN THE StarF.—troth. We regret to record the 
death of Mr. W. F. Chapman, which occurred in the Royal 
Victoria Hospital, on June 12th, 1899. He was surely a 
loyal, devoted, unselfish officer, and served the Association 
with a single aim and purpose. At his own request the 
funeral service was held in the Association building, and he 
was interred in Association lot in Mount Royal Cemetery. 

Mr. F. E. Burgess, from Stratford, was secured as Libra- 
rian in June last. Mr. F. A. Crowe, Junior Secretary, resigned 


16 


in November to enter business, but he has continued | 
active co-operation with the Junior Department and oth 
brenches of the work. Mr. Geo. E. Winter, of Halifax, to, 
the position as Secretary of the Junior Department a 
Assistant Physical Director, in October, 1899, from which 
resigned to enter business in April. He also is now a yal 
able addition to our volunteer force. Mr. John Brown, fro 
the West-End Branch, Toronto, succeeded Mr. G. E. Wint 
as Junior Department Secretary. Mr. John Roy, Members 

Secretary, has leave of absence to take a four months’ spe 

course of study at Moody’s School, Mount Hermon, Ma 
He expects to return on September 1st. These frequ 
changes in the office staff greatly increase the difficulties 
effective supervision of the work. 


Supreme Aim.—t1ith. The supreme aim of the Associatis 
is to bring men to a personal knowledge of Jesus Christ 
their Saviour, and to lead them to give their lives in lo 
service to Him, Also to create and foster a personal desi 
ior the daily reading and study of the Scriptures. All ¢ 
other privileges offered in the Educational, Social 
Physical Departments are a means: towards this end, E 
while hundreds of young men have been benefited by th 
means, the spirit and aim of the work is that they may be 
to the consideration of higher things, and we are glad 
know that in the lives of a number of our members this res} 
has been attained. 7

The following extracts taken from letters bear testimony 
to the practical value of the Association work :-— : 
“Dear Mr. Bunce, 


“T came to Montreal ten years ago sto enter one of the 
engineering firms as an apprentice. My first acquaintances 


19 


were made through the Association, but I did not become a 
fe eober until the Building was opened on Dominion Square. 
oe my apprenticeship proceeded the desire to improve my- 
celf became greater, and I took advantage of the opportunity 
afiorded through the evening classes. The success which 
attended my studies in these classes attracted the attention of 
friends, who thereby became more interested in my progress. 
On the completion of my apprenticeship the way opened for 
me to take a University course in McGill, which I have 
-recently completed. It has been my privilege to serve on 
some of the Committees of the Association, where I have 
been greatly benefited, especially on account of the class of 
young men whom I have met amongst the workers ; men 
‘yho came forward with the hand of fellowship, and have 
roved themselves to be friends indeed. 

“Looking back over my ten years’. connection with the 
Association, and the opportunity it has afforded for advance- 
ment, through the educational classes, and through the social 
and spiritual work of the Association, and especially in the 
fellowship with young men, there is rolled up a debt which I 
can never again repay. I have gained a higher ideal and aim 
in life. 

“ With best wishes for its success. 

“Yours sincerely, WEYee 


“Dear Mr. BUDGE, 

“JT am glad to acknowledge the benefits which have come 
to me through the Association, both educational, physical 
and spiritual, more _especially the last two. It is due to the 
‘Association and its officers that I am in a business position 
to-day, and I greatly appreciate the deep personal interest 
which has been taken in me. Young men who want to get 
the largest benefit should certainly be directed to the Young 
Men’s Christian Association, as T do not know where any one 
can find an organization offering the use of a first class gym- 
nasium and_ baths, socials, receptions, lectures, concerts, 
Bible classes, etc., and in the summer an ideal camp, and all 
kinds of clubs for the membership fee charged. 

“So long as I live and am where an Association exists you 
will always find my name enrolled as a member. 

“Yours sincerely, H.G.B.” 


* Dear Mr. BUDGE, 
“T came to the city last September, almost a total 
stranger, but with a letter of introduction from the Secretary 


20 


of the St. John Association. I soon became acquainted 
the Building, and I appreciate the reception which 
accorded to me, and the interest taken in me from the f; § 
“It has -been my privilege to attend regularly at 
Young Men’s Meeting on Saturday evening, and the Y, 
Men’s Bible Class on Sunday afternoon. These are 
interesting and instructive, and have been a very great | 
to me, ; 
“The Reading Room, with its splendid supply of 
and magazines, has enabled me to spend many a profit 
hour, as also the Library. One of the greatest advantage 
have found in the Association is, a place where you ea 
and feel that all its influences are helpful, that the youn 
with whom you come in contact are trying to live moral, 
right, clean lives, and are companions and friends you 1 
not be ashamed of. To any young man who is away 
home as I am, and in a strange city, it seems to me the. 
ciation is invaluable because of all the home-like and 
privileges which it offers. ‘ 
“Believe me, Yours faithfully, W.B.K 


“DEAR Mr. Bunce, i 
“As I am compelled to return to England in the mort 
I want to tell you, that after a stay of six months in th { 
of Montreal, I feel like leaving home in parting fro 
Young Men’s Christian Association, and the many 
whom I have met with there. In addition to the 
privileges, I have learned that Jesus Christ is our best 
in whom to trust, and to be our guide in-all things. 
“ Wishing God’s richest blessing to rest upon the wi 
the Association. a 
“Yours faithfully, A.W. 


“DEAR Mr. Bunce, “ 
“This Association has been one of the greatest influet 
in my life. I am more than thankful for the many 
physical, and educational advantages which it has af 
me, and by means of it I have been very greatly ben 
But especially I feel grateful for the opportunities whi 
Bible study classes of the religious services have offere 
personal improvement and development. 
“Yours sincerely, T.M.

MEMBERSHIP COMMITTEE, 


The work of the Committee during the past year has b 
terized mainly by faithful consecutive effort from month 
in the way of following up renewals and solicitation of new 
with an entire absence of any abnormal or special efforts, 
advertising the privileges by use of printed matter, the 

The policy of the Committee in reference to the Sust 
bership has been steadily adhered to. It is gratifying to r 


29 


mber of Sustaining members, which two years ago stood at 
nu! ear 120, NOW stands at 180. We are also glad to report that 
al tion of the Board of Directors, passed early in the year, 
pe ining ticket was made to cover all club and educational 
4 This change was welcomed by many who wished to make 
ment cover their use of the Association privileges. From 
aS BS dime the attention of our members has been called to the 
ame fllity of becoming sustaining members, in view of the oppor- 
desirab’ this ticket affords of contributing to the support of the 
apart from the question of the use of the privileges. 
his connection it is pleasing to note that a number of our 
ot sd members have set the very commendable example of volun- 
y ee taking out sustaining tickets, thus evincing in a tangible way 
ir appreciation of the Association. 
Jn reference to the work for the coming year, while we are grate- 
sa] for all that has been accomplished, the Committee would suggest 
a ¢ each department Committee consider the adoption of a policy 
oking to a definite increase - of our membership through their 
operation. In particular it is stiggested that the Social, Physical, 
cational and Junior departments take up the question with the 
‘mn of increasing the number of men using the privileges in their 
wepective departments. We believe that a little earnest. co-operation 
jn this way would easily bring our membership up to the 2,000 mark.

MEN’S MEETING. 


The Men’s Meeting on Sunday Afternoon at 4.15, started Oct. 
th, and ran continuously to April 29th. Twenty-nine meetings, 
Ph a total attendance of 3,698, or an average of 127. 
For three or four years past this meeting has not been regularly 
eld, but from the experience of the past winter, your Committee 
' feels that it is needed. ; : 
The addresses were of an exceptionally high type.—Jesus as the 
Saviour of man was the theme of them all. The music, under the 
“able leadership of Mr. J. J. Bell, was of the greatest assistance. 
‘Among the out-of-town speakers who may be specially mentioned 
were, Bishop Baldwin and Prof. W. W. White. A very impressive 
Memorial Service to the late Mr. D. L. Moody, participated in by 
many of Mr. Moody’s warm friends, was held on Dee. gist. 


A. M. MACKAY, 
Chairman. 


HOSPITAL COMMITTEE. 


_yarious ways. , : 

Thanks to several ladies and gentlemen from Mountain Street 
Methodist Church Choir, and to one of our own members who 
donated a small folding organ, we have been able to hold some very 
enjoyable song services, which have been much appreciated by the 
inmates, as well as by ourselves. 

_A short service was also held at the Homeopathic Hospital on 
Sunday afternoons during the months May to October.

BIBLE STUDY DEPARTMENT. 


At the beginning of the year it was decided to organize the 
ble Study of the Association into a Department to be administered 
a Bible Study Department Committee, as is the case with the 
ial, Educational, Physical and Junior Departments of the Asso- 
ation. It was felt that this would bring it into greater prominence 
i the Association life. It is our conviction that we should have as 
hy men studying the Bible in the Association as are enrolled in 
either the Educational or Gymnasium Classes. It is only fair to say 
Mat we have been much encouraged at the progress made in this 

ection this year. Early in October a Prospectus of the Bible 
sses for the season was issued and widely circulated, both among 
f members and the young men of our City. This, together with 
Personal efforts of the Committee and the Secretaries, resulted

SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee has arranged for the social features in the 
Building, as follows :— ; 

On September 28th, the Opening Exercises in connection with the 
Educational Classes took place, at which the Committee assisted in 
providing the programme and refreshments. 


On the evening of Thanksgiving Day, a Supper was given to 
Young Men away from home. About 65 sat down to the bounti- 
fully laden tables, so kindly provided and waited upon by members 
of the Ladies’ Committee. After these had been well patronized the 
usual toasts were proposed and responded to. We were also favored 
with solos by Mr. J. Ritchie Bell, which were most thoroughly 
enjoyed. The Thanksgiving Supper is always an interesting feature 
oi the Committee’s work, and is heartily appreciated by the young 
men. It doubtless does much to recall similar occasions spent amid 
the home surroundings and to strengthen the home ties. 


The usual Fall Reception was held on November 2nd, for new 
members, when an enjoyable programme was arranged for in the 
Association Hall. 

The Annual Reception on New Year’s Day was more successful 
than ever. The number who visited the Building during the day was 
about 2,400. The Physical Department members gave an exhibition 
on the floor of the Gymnasium, followed by an exciting game of 
Basket Ball. Mr. L. O, Armstrong gave a most interesting illus- 
trated Lecture in Association Hall, on the Rocky Mountains and 
Canadian scenery, as touched by the Canadian Pacific Railway. A 
splendid collection of views of Canadian scenery was kindly loaned 
by the Grand Trunk Railway and displayed in the Reading Room. 


The Camera Club arranged an exhibition of Amateur Photo- 
graphy in the Board Room, which attracted’ great attention. We 
are glad to note year by year the increasing excellence of their work 
in amateur photography on the part of many of our Association 
members. 

In the evening the usual Concert was given in Association Hall, 
and it was a decided success. 

To accommodate the overflow, Illustrated Views of English and 
Scottish Scenery were shown in the Lecture Hall, by our President, 
Mr. C. T. Williams. The Orchestra rendered most acceptable service 
‘in the afternoon and evening, and the ladies, to whom great credit 
is due, received as usual in the Lecture Hall. 


We are glad to see that the New Year’s Reception is looked for- 

ward to by many of our old members and friends as an opportunity 
fora hearty hand-shake and re-union, and that the spirit of the day 
thoroughly entered into by our new members. 


On January 18th a Patriotic Farewell Service was held on the 

Casion of the departure of Mr. T. F. Best, Secretary of the Brant- 

rd Association, with the Second Canadian Contingent for South 
ca. A programme of patriotic selections was arranged, and we 

€ indebted to the Rey. O. W. Howard, M.A., for a stirring address. 
Occasion was one of unusual interest. 


At the Educational Closing, April 5th, the Committee co-operated 


the Educational Committee in arranging programme and 
hments,

THE STRANGERS’ TEA COMMITTEE sustained a sey, 
loss in the removal of our friend and co-worker, Mr. Geo. Ja 
from the city, and his departure was received with profound re 
During the year the work has been continued regularly with y 
and enthusiasm. Nine Sunday Evening Teas have been held, 
an average attendance of 30. These teas are held once a month, 
Sunday evening from 5.15 to 6.30, to which are invited young 
Strangers in the city. Usually one of the Directors of the Assoe 
tion presides. After supper a half-hour of social intercou 
enjoyed, taking the form of introductions and remarks from 
present, and devotional exercises, adjourning for the evening ¢ 
services. The Committee feel that the Strangers’ Tea is fulfill: 
most important service in the life of the Association, and 
encouraged constantly by evidences of its good work,

EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


Courses of study were conducted during the season, Octobi 
to March 3oth, in ten subjects, as indicated in statistical sta 
below. 266 different members were enrolled in these classes, 
some members took more than one class the total enrolment 
the classes was 360. The principal changes introduced th 
were: (1) the addition of Elementary and Advanced C 
German ; (2) the enlargement of the course in Advanced 
(3) the abandonment of the advanced class in Shorthand ; 
the addition of advanced class in Electricity. The system | 
fees, as followed last year, was continued with minor chang 
addition, the full membership ticket was required for adm 


a lad 


ol 


the classes instead of the limited ticket as last year. This change 
may account for a smaller enrolment in some of the classes, but we 
are glad to report that the interest on the part of the students has 
been well sustained. 48 wrote on the International Examinations 
this year- Of these, 31 passed, having obtained 75 per cent. or over.

JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


In reporting upon the last season’s work amongst the Boys, your 
Committee feel that they have come through a year of somewhat new 
and difficult experiences, and in looking back over the ground that 
has been covered, can see many points where improvements might 
be made. There are, however, very many things for which to be 
thankful. The interest in the work. still continues, and the good 
influences of the Boys’ Meeting and Bible Class have told in the lives 

of a number of our members. 

The membership roll now has 178 names, as against 169 last year. 
A private post card, under the title of “The Junior Monthly ” 
has been published during the past seven or eight months, and has 
served to keep the membership posted as to events of interest. 

The Committee regret the withdrawal of Messrs. Geo. C. Wells 
and Geo. Lyman, through pressure of business, from active service 
on the Committee. 

The RELIGIOUS Meetings have been conducted every week 
since the last Annual Report, and the interest of the Boys has been 
most encouraging. Efforts are made to induce the boys to attend 
regularly, and occasional social features have been introduced to 
this end. We have also commenced using the Association Lantern, 
by throwing on the canvas pictures illustrating Bible characters and 
events. This will probably be continued at intervals, as its first trial 
has certainly been a success. 

One Bible Class, F. A. Crowe, Leader, has been conducted on 
Sunday afternoons throughout the winter, with an average attend- 
ance of five. 

Hospital Services have been conducted on the first Sunday of 
nearly every month, in the General Hospital, and flowers and maga- 
zines distributed amongst the patients. 

Interest in our representative, Mr. David McConaughy, in India, 
and in Foreign Missions generally, has been aroused through a tall 
given by Prot. W. W. White, while in Montreal, and the boys have 
commenced giving definitely to these good objects. 

The SOCIAL Work has benefited, and the attractiveness of the 
rooms increased by the addition of new tables and games, and a new 
carpet, for which our hearty thanks are due to the Finance Com- 
mittee. The Library has been well used, and the magazines largely 
patronized. Several social gatherings, entertainments and receptions 
have been held during the winter and spring, with good results. 

PHYSICAL.—The Gymnasium Classes have been well attended, 
the boys, especially in the evening classes, shewing: great interest in 
their work. Basket Ball tournaments have again been successfully 
organized and carried through, keen competition having been in- 
duced by the presentation of a couple of banners from the ladies. 

The Snow Shoe Club had a very interested, although small mem- 
bership. Our Annual Sleigh Drive was one of the largest on record. 

During the warmer months the Bicycle Club had several good 
runs, and this year's organization promises to be an active one. The 
boys also had a very enjoyable Picnic to Ile Gros Bois. 

The JUNIOR CAMP was held during the first two weeks of 
July, with very beneficial results, we believe spiritually as well as 


physically. There were no accidents or sicknesses of any kind, and 


of satisfaction encourage the Committee to 
better results this year, 


The Department feels a great loss in the death of Mr, ir 
Chapman, who took so much interest in the welfare of the Camp

LADIES’ COMMITTEE. 


The Committee has continued its work along the lines which were 
begun last year. The idea of forming an auxiliary was discussed, 
but given up, and the number on the Committee limited to twenty. 
Several ladies have been asked to pledge an annual subscription of 
$1.00 or more. In this way we-are assured of at least $150.00 yearly, 
from about go contributors. 

The Committee have had _ the parlor carpets renovated, new 
curtains and shades hung, and the furniture repaired. They have 
assisted the Association in its social work to some extent. Besides 
providing for the refreshments at several smaller affairs, they have 
arranged for the Thanksgiving Tea, the New Year's Reception and 
the Annual Committee-men’s Tea. For the closing Socials of the 
Educational and Physical Departments, they asked the assistance of 
the Ladies of Knox and Erskine, Mountain Street Methodist and 
Douglas Churches. 

One new feature of the work is that of the Flower Sub-Committee, 
who remember with gifts of flowers the young men members of the 
Association, and others, who may be ill, especially those boarding in 
the city, or in the hospital. 

Another new feature is assisting at the Strangers’ Teas. One or 
two of the members of this Committee are to be present at each of 
these gatherings to do what they can to make it homelike and 
enjoyable for the guests

PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee are pleased to report that substantial progress has 
marked the past year. The attendance has increased, the facilities 
and advantages of the Department have been more appreciated, and 
the Gymnasium classes have had a better average attendance than 
last year. The increased enthusiasm has been even more marked 
in the out-door exercises, such as Cycling, Baseball, Tennis, 
Athietics, ete. 

The leaders have excelled themselves, from the Physical Director, 
whose development from the bachelor to the benedict has been 
enthusiastically received throughout the Association. Mr. and Mrs. 
Ball will together share in future the affection and honors which the 
Physical Director has always so well merited. 


LEADERS’ CORPS. 
W. G. BURREUD R-. eemeenre cot = President. 


The Leaders’ Corps has fully sustained its reputation, the mem- 
bers rendering willing assistance to the Physical Director on the 
Gymnasium floor, in the Examining Room and in Exhibition work. 
The Leaders’ Headquarters and Library Room is a new resort in 
which weekly discussions are held. 

On New Year’s Day the Leaders gave an Exhibition in the 
Gymnasium, and again at the Riverside School, Point St Charles, on 
fhe 20th April. The Fifth Annual Banquet came off on February 
zend. Five new leaders have been added to the corps, which now

TENNIS CLUB. 
E. W.. SHARP 405 .< os ee ae «. President, 


The Club now has a membership of 45, and had a very successful 
season, largely the result of the centrally located grounds obtained 
on the corner of Bishop and St. Catherine Streets. The Club 
defeated the West End Club, tied St. Lambert, and defeated the 
Montreal Intermediate by four games to one. Although unusually 


heavy expenses were incurred the season has shown a slight balance 
on the right side. 


BASEBALL CLUB. 
Wiphl (Gane rola Secretary-Treasurer. 


Organized last June with a membership of 31, and played on the 
Montreal Baseball Park, Monday and Friday evenings. Out of four 
games with outside teams, this Club won three. Its finances closed 
with a small balance of 54 cents on hand.

ATHLETIC CLUB. 


1G. WEBBER Ite, se ee era moy eos President. 


The use of the Baseball grounds two evenings a week greatly 
fostered this branch of out-door sport. The membership increased 
from 13 to 31, and great interest was taken throughout. Some mem- 
bers took part in the M.A.A.A. Spring and Fall Handicaps, and 
made a fair showing. 

The Annual Field Day on September 21st was the best we have 
vet had. Admission to the grounds was by complimentary ticket, 
and there were 120 entries by about 50 men. The events were all 
keenly contested. We heartily thank those who generously contri- 
buted to the prizes. Our cash balance is $4.80. 


HOCKEY CLUB. 
ft UL SBENEDICE aie ctprs om pang an tiers President. 


The Hockey Club has had its most successiul year. The players 


had the use of the “Arena” rink three different hours each week. 
The membership reached 54. Five teams were organized from this 
number, and a series of matches scheduled among themselves. Team 
No. 1, captained by Mr. Wm. Field, won the series, and have the 
proud distinction of being the “ Hockey Champions” for 1900, and 
hold the handsome silver trophy offered by the Club. " The repre- 
sentative team played several matches with outside teams, and only 
had one goal scored against them. The Club have a credit balance 


of $15.10.

RAILROAD DEPARTMENT. 


The Railroad Department is located at the Sub-way, corner of 
Wellington and Richmond Streets, Point St. Charles. A joint work 
is carried on there for railway men and city young men of that 
district. This Department was organized in 1897, but the close of 
this fiscal year marks the first full year with its newer equipment, of 
beds, baths, lunch room, etc., to meet the needs of railway men lying 
over at this point. The additional conveniences were made possible 
in March of last year by a generous increase of the appropriation of 
the Grand Trunk Railway System, and appropriation from the City 
Association. During the year the membership has increased from 
65 to 146. About 77 per cent. of these are railway men, representing 
the Grand Trunk, Central Vermont, Canada Atlantic, Intercolonial, 
and Delaware and Hudson Railroads. 

The Financial Statement and the facts, herewith, give a good 
idea of the year’s work, but by way of explanation, we add the 
following :— 

During the month of August four beds were added to partly meet 
the demand for more Rest Rooms. More beds were needed, but no 
further additions could be made for lack of room. As many as 
twenty men have found rest in ten beds during twenty-four hours. 
During the month of July a Men’s Bible Class was organized, meet- 
ing every Sunday morning at 9.30 o'clock. In December a Women’s 
Auxiliary was organized, and now has a membership of 41. They 
have been of much assistance to the Department. Several social 
occasions have been given under their auspices. They have aided 
substantially too by their contribution to the current expenses of the 
Department, and the appearance and convenience of the building has 
been much improved by their gift of furniture, decorations and 
time. At the opening of the year the Financial Statement showed 
unpaid bills to the amount of $581.63. We close the year with all 
bills paid. There is a reasonable hope that before the next annual 
meeting this Department will be quartered in a new building, 
modern in its equipment, and fully adapted to meet the needs of the 
railway men and young men of this section of the City. With sin- 
cere gratitude to our Heavenly Father for His blessing and help in 
the year passed, we look forward to the new year with faith for 
greater things by His help. 

W. H. BLACKALLER, F. S. MORRISON, 


Chairman. Secretary.

THE WOMAN’S AUXILIARY, 


On December 7th of last year a company of nineteen women of 
Point St. Charles and vicinity met to consider ways and means by 
which they could assist in the work of the Railroad Department of 
the Young Men’s Christian Association. This meeting resulted in 
the formation of the Woman’s Auxiliary of the Railroad Department 
of the Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal, and has now 
a membership of forty-one. The object of the organization was not 
to secure Association privileges for themselves, but to aid in every 
way possible in making the work of the Association efficient in all its 
departments. During the few months since the inception of the 
Wonian’s Auxiliary it has done much towards accomplishing the 
purpose of its organization. The following is a very general state- 
ment of the events held under their auspices : “ Open House,’ New 
Year’s Day, one Social Evening, one Concert for the benefit of the 
Auxiliary fund, and the Anniversary Supper, which was an event of 
a high order ; the tables were beautifully decorated and the service 
was excellent in all its appointments, the Orchestra of the Dominion 
Square Association rendered delightful music, and the crowning 
feature of the evening was the presentation, by Mr. C. T. Williams, 
of an elegant roll-top desk, for the Association, which had been 
purchased by the Auxiliary and given as a surprise. The Auxiliary 
desire to take this opportunity to expréss their appreciation of the 
valuable assistance rendered them in their work by Messrs. S. 
Carsley, C. Alexander and Tees & Co. They have held one Gospel 
Temperance meeting for women only. Three of their members 
attended the Annual Conference of the Woman’s Auxiliaries of 
Ontario and Quebec, held at Woodstock, Ont. The following is a 
roll of the membership of the Auxiliary :— 


Mrs. WatreR Minair, .. .. .. .. .. President. 

Mrs. CuHaRLEs CoRNER, .. .. .. .. .. Ist Vice-President. 

Mrs. Davin Barton, .. .. .. .. .. .. 2nd Vice-President.

Mr. M. E. IncAtts, President Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago & St. 
Louis, and of the Chesapeake & Ohio Railways, says :— 

“T am a firm believer in the Young Men’s Christian Association, 
and especially in its Railroad branch. I have had some experience 
with it in the West and South, and it has grown steadily in my appre- 
ciation and favor. It enables railway employees to obtain some 
social life at a moderate expense. It takes the place of the beer 
saloon and other places of resort of questionable character. I often 
hear objections to it on the ground that it is semi-religious and not 
entirely social. That is one of the reasons why I like. it. It is the 
one controlling feature that has tended to make it a success. I 
would not object if our large and wealthy clubs had more of that 
element. The word ‘Christian’ is so comprehensive that it ought 
not to disturb the sectarian notions of any one; and the man who 
is not a Christian—in the broad definition of that term—I have no 
use for. 

“The Railroad Department of the Association has succeeded wher- 
ever it has gone. It has accomplished what no other institution has 
in this country ; it has secured subscriptions from railway corpora- 
tions, from wealthy men, from the employees, and has kept up the 
interest of the people in iis work from its inception until now. It 
has done as much to bring the employer and employee together as 
any institution. There may be some other organization or plan that 
has made as much progress, but I have failed to find it. I have never 
yet found any organization that combined so well the interests of 
railway men and the owners as this has done.”
